title: A young patient after a two-valve operation
subtitle: A 29-year-old man admitted to the CTICU after a long operation on two valves and a conduit, with a new murmur the intensivist is not sure how to interpret.
objectives: Describe the anatomy the Ross procedure leaves behind (pulmonary autograft in the aortic position, homograft in the RVOT, two reimplanted coronary buttons, two RVOT suture lines) and name the specific ways each element can fail in the first 72 hours.
Distinguish the expected early echo findings after a Ross (trivial to mild neo-aortic regurgitation, a modest homograft gradient) from the findings that demand a call to the surgeon.
Explain why systemic hypertension is a uniquely harmful insult to a fresh autograft and build a blood pressure and inotrope strategy around that fact.
Work through new ST changes with hypotension on postoperative day 1 as a coronary button problem until proven otherwise, and state the threshold for imaging and for return to the operating room.
Summarize the long-term failure modes of both valves well enough to counsel the patient on what the ICU course does and does not mean for durability.

stages.title: Presentation
stages.narrative:
A 29-year-old man arrives in the CTICU at 19:40 after an operation that took most of the day. He is a competitive amateur cyclist with a bicuspid aortic valve and severe aortic regurgitation, a mildly dilated LV, and a normal ascending aorta. He has no other medical history. [REVIEW]

The surgical note describes a pulmonary autograft placed in the aortic position as a full root replacement, with both coronary buttons reimplanted, the autograft wrapped in an external support graft at the sinotubular junction and annulus, and a cryopreserved pulmonary homograft placed in the right ventricular outflow tract. Cardiopulmonary bypass and cross-clamp times were long. He came off bypass on a low-dose inotrope and a vasopressor. Intraoperative TEE after separation from bypass reportedly showed trivial neo-aortic regurgitation, a small gradient across the homograft, and normal biventricular function. [REVIEW]

On arrival he is intubated, warm, and well perfused. The mean arterial pressure is comfortably in range on a low vasopressor dose. Chest tube output is modest and serous. The overnight resident, examining him at handoff, hears a soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border and a short diastolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, and asks whether these are expected. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Before you look at anything else, describe the anatomy this patient now has: what was moved, what was added, and where the suture lines and reimplantations are. Then list the specific ways this reconstruction can fail in the first 72 hours that would not apply to a conventional aortic valve replacement. Commit before revealing.
questions.modelAnswer:
The Ross procedure uses the patient's own pulmonary valve and root as a living substitute for the diseased aortic valve, and replaces the pulmonary valve with a homograft. The intensivist inherits a reconstruction with several more failure points than a standard AVR.

**What was done.**

- The native aortic valve and root were excised and the coronary ostia were mobilized as buttons.
- The pulmonary root (valve, sinuses, a short segment of main pulmonary artery) was harvested from the RVOT. The harvest passes close to the first septal perforator of the LAD, which can be injured during dissection. [REVIEW]
- The autograft was sewn into the aortic position as a full root replacement: a proximal suture line at the annulus and a distal anastomosis to the ascending aorta. The two coronary buttons were reimplanted into the autograft sinuses. In this patient the surgeon also placed an external support graft to limit dilation. The root replacement technique is the most widely used today, but two older alternatives exist: the subcoronary technique (autograft valve only, implanted inside the native root, no coronary reimplantation) and the inclusion or cylinder technique (autograft placed inside the preserved native aortic root, which acts as a natural wrap). The three techniques distribute risk differently: the subcoronary approach avoids coronary reimplantation but is technically demanding and is less commonly done, while the full root approach exposes the autograft wall to systemic pressure without native support unless reinforced. Mazine and colleagues review this in their 2018 state-of-the-art paper. [VERIFY]
- A pulmonary homograft was placed in the RVOT with a proximal suture line to the right ventricular infundibulum and a distal anastomosis to the pulmonary artery bifurcation.

**The failure points that are specific to this operation.**

1. **Two coronary reimplantations.** Each button can kink, twist, be placed under tension, bleed, or thrombose. This is the same risk as any root replacement (Bentall, valve-sparing root) and is the most dangerous early complication. Proximity of the autograft harvest to the first septal perforator adds a second mechanism of anterior septal ischemia that has nothing to do with the buttons. [REVIEW]
2. **A fresh pulmonary root under systemic pressure.** The autograft wall was designed for a pressure one-fifth of what it now sees. It will remodel over months, but in the first days a hypertensive surge stretches a suture line and a tissue that are not yet adapted. This is the physiological basis for the blood pressure strategy in the next stage. [REVIEW]
3. **Two additional suture lines on the right side.** The proximal and distal homograft anastomoses are bleeding sites behind the heart and under the left lung that can be hard to see on re-exploration and are often the reason a Ross patient returns to the operating room for bleeding. The El-Hamamsy trial reported a re-exploration rate for bleeding of 12 percent in the autograft arm versus 4 percent with homograft root replacement. [REVIEW]
4. **Homograft obstruction.** Early RVOT obstruction from kinking, size mismatch, or compression against the sternum is uncommon but will present as RV strain, and its murmur is the one the resident heard at the left upper sternal border.
5. **A long bypass and cross-clamp time.** This is a two-root operation. Expect more vasoplegia, more coagulopathy, and more myocardial stunning than for a routine AVR of the same age. The 2010 randomized trial reported a mean bypass time of 163 minutes for autograft versus 117 minutes for homograft root replacement. [REVIEW]

The conceptual shift for the fellow: this is not a valve replacement with a murmur. It is a double root reconstruction with four anastomoses, two coronary reimplantations, and a living tissue under the wrong pressure. Every early problem should be mapped back to one of those elements.

questions.prompt: Why did the surgeon and cardiologist choose this operation for this patient rather than a mechanical or bioprosthetic AVR, and what did the patient accept in return? Name the alternatives and say what each would have cost him.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Best answer: In a young, active patient with a bicuspid valve, no ascending aortic disease, and a strong wish to avoid anticoagulation, the Ross offers a living, hemodynamically normal valve with the best long-term survival signal of any aortic valve substitute, at the cost of a bigger operation and two valves that can both fail.** The 2020 ACC/AHA guideline gives the Ross a limited place in adults, essentially as a reasonable option in selected young patients at experienced centers, and the 2021 ESC/EACTS guideline treats it similarly. The 2025 EACTS expert consensus statement is considerably more enthusiastic. [REVIEW]

The case for the Ross rests on four things:

- **Survival.** The El-Hamamsy randomized trial (Lancet 2010) compared autograft to homograft root replacement and found 10-year survival of 97 percent versus 83 percent, with autograft survival matching the general population. Mazine and colleagues (Circulation 2016) and Buratto and colleagues (JACC 2018, 20-year survival 94 percent versus 84 percent in matched pairs) reported better late survival with the Ross than with mechanical AVR in propensity-matched cohorts. These are observational comparisons with the exception of the Lancet trial, and selection bias toward healthier Ross patients is a real concern. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]
- **No anticoagulation.** A mechanical valve commits him to warfarin for life, with the bleeding and thromboembolism burden that carries, at an age where he will cycle, travel, and have children. The German Ross Registry reports low rates of thromboembolism, hemorrhage, and endocarditis. [REVIEW]
- **Hemodynamics.** The autograft is a living, competent, unobstructed root with normal flow characteristics, which matters for exercise capacity and for LV remodeling after years of regurgitation.
- **Growth and adaptation.** The living autograft can adapt, which matters most in children but is cited as a benefit of a viable valve in adults as well. [REVIEW]

What the alternatives would have cost him:

- **Mechanical AVR.** Durable, a single operation in most cases, and widely performed. The price is lifelong anticoagulation, a small but real annual stroke and bleeding risk, and a valve click. For a 29-year-old the cumulative risk over 50 years is not trivial. This remains the guideline default for young adults who accept anticoagulation.
- **Bioprosthetic AVR.** No anticoagulation, but a 29-year-old will outlive it, probably more than once, and structural valve degeneration is faster in the young. A valve-in-valve strategy is possible but is not a long-term plan for someone with 50 years to live. Mazine and colleagues (JACC 2022) reported better outcomes with the Ross than with bioprosthetic AVR. [REVIEW]
- **Homograft root.** The Lancet trial answers this directly: worse survival and much worse freedom from reoperation.
- **Valve repair.** Bicuspid valve repair is possible for regurgitation in selected anatomy, but durability is variable and the surgeon judged his leaflets unrepairable. [REVIEW]

What he accepted in return: a longer operation with more bleeding risk, two valves that can both fail (autograft dilation and regurgitation, homograft stenosis), the near certainty of surveillance for life, and a meaningful probability of reoperation on one or both valves over several decades. The honest framing, which the fellow should be able to deliver to his family tonight, is that he traded a predictable problem (anticoagulation) for a less predictable one (two valves to watch), on the strength of survival data that are strong but mostly observational and that come from expert centers.

stages.title: New data
stages.narrative:
You go to the bedside with the night cardiology fellow and a transthoracic probe. The neo-aortic valve is a trileaflet structure in the aortic position with good excursion. There is a thin central jet of regurgitation that you would call mild at most. The autograft root dimensions at the annulus, sinuses, and sinotubular junction are recorded and are similar to the intraoperative TEE measurements. There is a modest peak gradient across the homograft with a thin turbulent jet, and the RV is normal in size with preserved function. There is no pericardial effusion. LV function is normal with no regional wall motion abnormality. [REVIEW]

The arterial pressure has risen over the past hour as he has warmed and the vasopressor has been weaned to off. His systolic pressure is now well above the range the surgeon wrote in the postoperative orders. He is lightly sedated and beginning to cough on the tube. [REVIEW]

The resident asks two things: whether the echo findings are reassuring, and what to do about the blood pressure.

questions.prompt: Sort the possible early echo findings after a Ross into expected and concerning. For each concerning finding, name the mechanism and the action. Then say whether tonight's study is reassuring.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Expected findings in the first days.**

- **Trivial or mild neo-aortic regurgitation.** The autograft valve is a normal pulmonary valve now exposed to diastolic systemic pressure. A thin central jet is common and is not by itself a concern. [REVIEW]
- **A modest gradient across the homograft.** A cryopreserved homograft is a biological conduit sized to the RVOT and will have some gradient, especially with a hyperdynamic circulation after bypass. The gradient tends to rise over years rather than days. [REVIEW]
- **Mild LV stunning and a mildly reduced RV after a long bypass run.** Both should recover within a day or two.
- **Autograft dimensions matching the intraoperative measurements.** The root should not have changed in eight hours.

**Concerning findings and what they mean.**

- **Significant (moderate or more) neo-aortic regurgitation.** Mechanisms are technical: commissural malalignment, a sinotubular junction that is too wide, an annulus that is too large for the autograft, or leaflet injury during harvest. Early significant AI on a fresh autograft usually means a return to the operating room, and the decision is the surgeon's. Call them tonight, not at rounds. [REVIEW]
- **Autograft root dilation on serial measurement.** The autograft is a pulmonary root under systemic pressure, and dilation is its main long-term failure mode (see the final stage). Acute change over hours in the ICU would suggest a hypertensive insult or a technical problem at a suture line and needs the surgeon's eyes on the images. [REVIEW]
- **A new regional wall motion abnormality.** Until proven otherwise this is a coronary button problem: kinking, tension, dissection at the ostium, or thrombosis. Anterior or anteroseptal hypokinesis after a Ross can also reflect injury to the first septal perforator during autograft harvest, which has the same urgency and a different fix. This finding is covered in the next stage. [REVIEW]
- **Homograft obstruction with RV strain.** A high gradient with a dilated, hypokinetic RV and a flattened septum points to kinking, compression, or a size mismatch. The RV tolerates acute obstruction poorly and this is also a surgical conversation.
- **Pericardial effusion with hemodynamic effect.** Two root suture lines plus two homograft anastomoses means more places to bleed than a standard AVR, and bleeding behind the heart can tamponade regionally without a large circumferential effusion.
- **A new or enlarging hematoma around the root or a flap in the ascending aorta.** Rare, but the distal autograft anastomosis is a potential dissection site.

**Is tonight's study reassuring?** Yes, for the valves. Mild AI, a modest homograft gradient, stable root dimensions, normal biventricular function, and no effusion is the expected picture. The caveat is that a transthoracic study in a ventilated patient a few hours after a sternotomy has limited windows. If the resident or fellow cannot see the root clearly, or cannot assess regional wall motion with confidence, the right answer is a TEE rather than a reassuring note built on poor images. [REVIEW]

What the study does not tell you: it does not predict the blood pressure problem that is developing at the same bedside, and it does not make tomorrow's ST changes any less likely. The comparison measurements recorded tonight are the baseline every later study will be judged against. Make sure they are written in the chart, not only in the echo report.

questions.prompt: His systolic pressure is now well above the surgeon's written target. Commit to a blood pressure strategy for the next 24 hours. State what makes hypertension more dangerous after a Ross than after a conventional AVR, which agents you would use and avoid, and how you would handle the inotrope he arrived on.
questions.modelAnswer:
**The physiology.** The autograft is a pulmonary root. Its wall is thinner and has a different elastin and collagen architecture than the aortic root it replaced, and it was built for a mean pressure of roughly one-fifth of the systemic value. It remodels toward an aortic phenotype over months, but in the first days and weeks it is a compliant tube under a pressure it was never meant to carry. The main late failure mode of the Ross is autograft dilation with secondary neo-aortic regurgitation, and most Ross surgeons believe that early hypertension accelerates it. That belief is physiologically sound and widely held, and it is also not supported by a randomized trial. The EACTS expert consensus statement and major Ross centers recommend strict blood pressure control early after the Ross and in the longer term, and it is standard practice at high-volume programs. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

A second reason is mechanical and immediate. There are four fresh suture lines on two roots, a reinforced sinotubular junction, and two coronary buttons. A pressure surge in the first hours is a bleeding risk at every one of them.

**The strategy.**

- **Target.** The surgeon's written target governs. Where none is written, the fellow should ask tonight rather than pick a number. A reasonable framing is a systolic range well below what you would tolerate after a routine AVR, with avoidance of both the surge and the trough. The actual numbers belong to the institution and the surgeon. [NMH protocol, insert]
- **Treat the cause first.** He is warming, waking, and coughing on the tube. Analgesia, sedation adequate to the ventilator, and attention to the bladder and to shivering will often fix the pressure before any antihypertensive is needed. Rewarming vasodilation will also return and the pressure may fall on its own, so avoid a long-acting agent that will still be working when it does.
- **Agents.** A short-acting intravenous beta blocker or a titratable vasodilator infusion are the usual choices, with the choice shaped by heart rate and by what the surgeon prefers. Beta blockade has a logic here beyond the pressure: it reduces the rate of pressure rise (dP/dt) and therefore the shear on the autograft wall, which is the same argument used for aortic dissection. Pure vasodilators drop the pressure but can raise dP/dt and heart rate, which is why many programs prefer a beta blocker as the first agent once the inotrope is off. Agent choice and dosing are institution-specific. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]
- **Avoid.** Inotropes that raise contractility and dP/dt without a hemodynamic need. He arrived on a low-dose inotrope because of a long bypass run, not because of ventricular failure, and his biventricular function is normal. The inotrope should be weaned off tonight, and if the pressure problem is being chased with an antihypertensive while an inotrope is still running, the inotrope should be stopped first. [REVIEW]
- **Avoid the trough too.** The coronary buttons depend on diastolic pressure. Over-treating to a low diastolic pressure in a patient with fresh reimplantations trades one risk for another.
- **Extubation.** Early extubation reduces the coughing and bucking that drive the surges, but an emergence with a hypertensive peak is exactly what you are trying to avoid. Plan the extubation so the pressure is controlled through it.

**The honest statement for the fellow.** Everything above except the suture-line bleeding risk is expert consensus and mechanistic reasoning. The long-term autograft dilation data are strong enough that no Ross surgeon will accept a hypertensive first night, but the specific target, the agent, and whether beta blockade is actually better than a vasodilator for the autograft are not established. That is an argument for following the surgeon's target closely, not for debating it at 02:00.

stages.title: Decision point
stages.narrative:
Postoperative day 1, 06:15. He was extubated at 02:00 with good pressure control on a low-dose beta blocker infusion. At 05:50 the nurse noted that he looked uncomfortable and asked for pain medication. Over the next 20 minutes his mean arterial pressure has fallen, his heart rate has risen, and the monitor shows new ST elevation in the anterior leads. He is pale, diaphoretic, and says his chest feels tight. Chest tube output has been low. [REVIEW]

A 12-lead ECG confirms anterior ST elevation. A stat bedside TTE shows a new anterior and anteroseptal wall motion abnormality with an LV that is now moderately reduced in function. The RV is unchanged. There is no significant effusion. The neo-aortic valve looks as it did last night. [REVIEW]

The surgeon is in the operating room with another patient. The interventional cardiologist is available. The CTICU attending is on the phone.

questions.prompt: What is the differential, which diagnosis is at the top and why, who do you call in what order, and what imaging decides the next step? Commit to the sequence.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Best answer: Compromise of the left coronary button (kinking, tension, ostial dissection, or thrombosis) until proven otherwise, with the surgeon called first and the catheterization laboratory activated in parallel.** Anterior ST elevation with a new anterior and anteroseptal wall motion abnormality on day 1 after a root replacement is a reimplanted left main until someone shows you otherwise. This is a surgical emergency that may need the operating room, not a STEMI pathway that happens to be in the CTICU. [REVIEW]

**The differential, in order of likelihood and danger.**

1. **Left coronary button compromise.** Mechanisms: kinking as the heart filled and the root took its final shape after the chest was closed, tension on the button, a hematoma or hemostatic material compressing the ostium, intimal injury at the button with dissection, or thrombosis at the anastomosis. The timing (after closure, after the heart has refilled, after the pressure changed with extubation) fits any of these.
2. **Injury to the first septal perforator during autograft harvest.** This causes anteroseptal ischemia with a patent left main. It presents the same way at the bedside and is distinguished at angiography. It is specific to the Ross and the fellow should name it so that an angiogram that shows a patent left main is not read as reassuring. [REVIEW]
3. **Coronary air or particulate embolism.** Usually declares itself in the operating room, not 12 hours later, but is possible after any open-chamber procedure. Typically affects the right coronary territory because of the anterior position of the ostium in the supine patient. The anterior distribution here argues against it.
4. **Coronary spasm.** Possible after any cardiac surgery and after coronary manipulation, usually responds to nitrates, and is a diagnosis of exclusion that should not delay imaging.
5. **Native coronary disease.** Unlikely at 29 without risk factors, and the preoperative imaging should answer this.
6. **Regional tamponade compressing the LAD territory or a coronary.** The effusion is not significant on TTE but a localized posterior collection can be missed. It does not explain the ECG as well as the alternatives.

**Who to call and in what order.**

- **The cardiac surgeon, immediately, through the operating room.** The surgeon's partner should be found if the primary surgeon cannot leave. This is their anastomosis and the decision between catheterization laboratory and direct return to the operating room is theirs.
- **The interventional cardiologist and the catheterization laboratory, at the same time.** Coronary angiography is the test that distinguishes a kinked or compressed button (which is usually fixed surgically) from a thrombosed ostium or a dissection (which may be treated with a stent, or may need surgery), from septal perforator injury (which is managed supportively), from spasm (nitrates). Activating the laboratory in parallel costs nothing if the surgeon decides to go straight to the operating room.
- **Perfusion and the operating room charge nurse,** so that a room and a circuit are ready either way.
- **The CTICU attending** is already on the phone. Mechanical support should be in the conversation now, not after he arrests.

**Imaging.** The bedside TTE has done its job: it showed the wall motion abnormality and excluded a large effusion. The next imaging is coronary angiography, and the decision is whether to do it in the catheterization laboratory or to open the chest. A TEE in the ICU or in the laboratory adds a look at the button origins, the root, and the anastomoses, and can show a dissection flap or a compressed ostium, but should not delay angiography. CT angiography is tempting because it shows the course of the button, but moving an unstable patient to the scanner is slow and it does not allow intervention. [REVIEW]

**The threshold for the operating room.** Low. If he becomes hemodynamically unstable, develops ventricular arrhythmia, or if angiography shows a mechanical button problem (kink, compression, tension) rather than a lesion that can be stented, he goes back to the operating room. Some surgeons will prefer to open the chest directly rather than send the patient to the laboratory, on the argument that a day-1 button problem after a Ross is nearly always mechanical and that angiography wastes time. Others want the roadmap first. There is no evidence base to adjudicate this and it will depend on the surgeon and the institution. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

**What you do while waiting.** Maintain diastolic pressure for coronary perfusion, which means the beta blocker infusion comes off and a vasopressor goes on if needed. Anticoagulation decisions (heparin now versus waiting for the surgeon) need the surgeon's input because the alternative diagnosis is bleeding at a suture line. Nitrates are reasonable if the pressure tolerates them and may unmask spasm. Have the defibrillator pads on. Have the sternotomy tray at the bedside. Do not give an inotrope to an ischemic ventricle with a fresh root unless the alternative is arrest.

questions.prompt: Angiography shows a patent left main with a kink at the button origin that improves with a change in loading conditions, and a diffusely narrowed LAD beyond it. The interventionalist offers to stent the ostium. The surgeon, now free, wants to re-explore. Make the argument for each, then say which you would support and why.
questions.modelAnswer:
**The argument for a stent.** It is immediate. The patient is already on the table with access. A stent across a kinked or compressed button ostium can restore flow within minutes and avoids a redo sternotomy on day 1 with its bleeding, infection, and myocardial injury cost. If he becomes unstable, the stent buys time for a controlled operation. Ostial stenting of reimplanted buttons has been reported after root replacement. [REVIEW]

**The argument for re-exploration.** The angiogram shows a mechanical problem: a kink that changes with loading. A stent treats the lumen, not the geometry. A kinked button under a stent may re-kink beyond the stent, the stent may be distorted by the suture line, and a stent in the ostium of a 29-year-old's left main commits him to antiplatelet therapy and to a lesion that will complicate every future root reoperation, which in a Ross patient is likely at some point. Surgical correction (releasing tension, repositioning the button, evacuating a hematoma, reimplanting the button if needed) fixes the mechanism. The surgeon knows exactly what was done and can see the cause. The diffuse narrowing in the LAD is most consistent with spasm or with distal hypoperfusion from the proximal kink and will likely resolve with correction of the proximal problem. [REVIEW]

**Which to support.** For a hemodynamically stable patient with a demonstrated mechanical kink on day 1, re-exploration by the operating surgeon is the better answer, and most Ross and root surgeons would say so. A stent is the right answer when the patient is unstable and the laboratory is where he is, or when the lesion is a thrombus or a dissection flap rather than a kink, or when the surgeon judges that reoperation on this root carries unacceptable risk. The fellow's job is to state the tradeoff clearly, make sure the surgeon and the interventionalist are talking to each other rather than to the fellow, and have the patient ready for either. [REVIEW]

Two things to add. First, if he arrests in the laboratory, the question is moot: the chest is opened there or he goes on mechanical support. Second, whichever path is chosen, the ventricle has been ischemic, and the next 24 hours will involve a stunned anterior wall, possible arrhythmia, and a lower threshold for mechanical support than he had yesterday. The fellow should think through what support device fits a patient with a fresh autograft root and a reimplanted button before it is needed. Anything that passes through the neo-aortic valve or sits in the root is a different conversation here than in a standard post-infarct patient. [REVIEW]

stages.title: The longer view
stages.narrative:
He returned to the operating room. The left button was found to be kinked by a combination of tension and a small hematoma. The button was mobilized and the hematoma evacuated. Flow was confirmed with a flow probe. He came off bypass easily. Postoperative day 4: he is extubated, off all support, on an oral beta blocker, with an anterior wall that is improving but not yet normal on echo. His troponin peaked and is falling. [REVIEW]

He is lucid and asking questions. He wants to know whether the operation has been damaged by what happened, whether he will cycle again, and whether he will need another operation. His partner wants to know what to watch for and how often he needs an echo.

questions.prompt: Explain the two-valve failure problem of the Ross procedure, say what surveillance he will need and why, and then write the paragraph you would say to him about what his ICU course does and does not mean for the durability of the operation.
questions.modelAnswer:
**The two-valve failure problem.** A Ross patient has two valves that can fail in different ways on different timelines.

- **The autograft dilates and leaks.** The pulmonary root under systemic pressure enlarges over years, mostly at the sinuses and sinotubular junction, and as it enlarges the leaflets lose coaptation and regurgitation develops. Risk factors identified in the registries and large series include a preoperative diagnosis of aortic regurgitation rather than stenosis, a large native annulus, a bicuspid valve with a dilated root, and hypertension. The German Ross Registry reports that autograft dysfunction is more pronounced in patients who had aortic insufficiency preoperatively and that aortic regurgitation and a large annulus are risk factors for reoperation. This patient had regurgitation and a bicuspid valve, which places him in a higher-risk group for autograft dilation, and is exactly why his surgeon placed external support and why his blood pressure will matter for the rest of his life. Reinforcement techniques (external graft wrap, inclusion technique, annular and sinotubular junction stabilization) are intended to prevent this and are an active area of disagreement. [REVIEW]
- **The homograft stenoses.** The cryopreserved homograft in the RVOT undergoes progressive calcification and shrinkage, driven partly by an immune response to the donor tissue. The gradient rises over years. Freedom from homograft reintervention is good in the first decade and declines after. The German Ross Registry notes that pulmonary homografts outperform bioprostheses in this position. Homograft failure is often addressed with a transcatheter pulmonary valve rather than a reoperation, which changes the calculation. [REVIEW]

The net result in the randomized trial was freedom from any valve reoperation of 94 percent at 13 years in the autograft arm, and in long-term registry data most patients remain free of reoperation for 15 to 20 years, with the reoperation rate higher than for mechanical valves and lower than for bioprostheses. [REVIEW]

**Surveillance.** Echocardiography at the first postoperative visit and then at an interval the surgeon and cardiologist set, with the first-year studies establishing the trajectory of the autograft dimensions and the homograft gradient. Thereafter annual or biennial imaging is typical, with attention to root dimensions, neo-aortic regurgitation, and the RVOT gradient. CT or MRI of the root is added at intervals or when echo windows are poor. The specific schedule follows the valve guidelines for prosthetic valve surveillance and local practice. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW] Lifelong blood pressure control is the one modifiable factor every Ross center emphasizes, and he will leave on a beta blocker or an equivalent whether or not he is hypertensive, as institutional practice rather than guideline. [REVIEW]

Endocarditis prophylaxis applies because he has prosthetic material and a homograft. [REVIEW]

**What to say to him.** Something like this:

"The operation itself is intact. The problem on the first morning was a kinked blood vessel where one of your coronary arteries was sewn back on, and that was fixed by freeing it up. The valve that was moved into the aortic position looks the way it should and the new valve on the right side is working. Part of the front of your heart was short of blood for a while and is recovering, and we expect it to keep recovering over the next weeks. That episode does not change how long the valves will last. What does change how long they last is your blood pressure, which is why you will be on medication for it, and whether we catch any change early, which is why you will have an echo every year for the rest of your life. Most people with this operation are free of further surgery for well over a decade and many for much longer, but you have two valves that can wear in different ways and it is likely you will need something done to one of them at some point, possibly through a catheter rather than another operation. Cycling is expected once the sternum has healed and the heart has recovered, and the surgeon will tell you when. Competitive effort will wait until the surveillance imaging confirms the root is stable." [REVIEW]

The counsel to avoid: telling him the autograft is a cure, telling him the ICU event has damaged the operation, or giving a number of years for either valve.

teachingPoints:
- The Ross is a double root reconstruction: two coronary reimplantations, four anastomoses, a living pulmonary root under systemic pressure, and a homograft on the right side. Every early problem should be mapped to one of those elements.
- Expected early echo findings are trivial or mild neo-aortic regurgitation and a modest homograft gradient. Moderate or greater AI, root dilation, a new regional wall motion abnormality, or RV strain from homograft obstruction are calls to the surgeon.
- Record the root dimensions on the first study. Every later study will be compared against them.
- Hypertension is a specific insult to the autograft wall and to four fresh suture lines. Treat the cause (pain, sedation, emergence), wean the inotrope first, favor agents that reduce dP/dt, and avoid both the surge and the trough. The target and the agent are the surgeon's and the institution's. [NMH protocol, insert]
- Anterior ST elevation with a new wall motion abnormality on day 1 is a reimplanted left coronary button until proven otherwise. Call the surgeon first and activate the catheterization laboratory in parallel. The Ross adds a second mechanism, first septal perforator injury during harvest, that an angiogram showing a patent left main does not exclude.
- A mechanical button problem (kink, tension, hematoma) in a stable patient is usually best fixed surgically. A stent is for the unstable patient in the laboratory or for a thrombus or dissection, and it complicates every future root operation in a patient who will probably need one.
- Both valves can fail: autograft dilation with AI (higher risk after preoperative AI, bicuspid valve, large annulus, hypertension) and homograft stenosis. Lifelong surveillance and blood pressure control are the two interventions the intensivist can set in motion from the ICU.
pitfalls:
- Treating a Ross as an AVR with a murmur. The failure points are those of two root replacements.
- Reassurance from a transthoracic study with poor windows in a ventilated patient. If the root and regional wall motion cannot be seen, get a TEE.
- Chasing a hypertensive emergence with a vasodilator while an inotrope is still running.
- Over-treating the pressure to a diastolic trough in a patient with two fresh coronary reimplantations.
- Running anterior ST elevation on day 1 down a medical STEMI pathway without calling the surgeon first.
- Reading a patent left main on angiography as excluding ischemia from the Ross when septal perforator injury during harvest is the alternative.
- Accepting an ostial stent on a kinked button in a stable patient without the surgeon in the room.
- Forgetting that the sternal re-entry, antiplatelet therapy, and any device that crosses the neo-aortic valve all carry different risks in a patient with a fresh autograft root.
- Telling the patient the operation is a cure, or that the ICU complication has damaged it.
controversies:
**Ross versus mechanical AVR in young adults.** The survival advantage of the Ross in the Toronto (Mazine 2016) and Melbourne (Buratto 2018) propensity-matched series and in the 2018 meta-analysis is consistent, but these are observational comparisons from expert centers with strong selection toward healthier Ross candidates. The only randomized trial (El-Hamamsy 2010) compared autograft with homograft, not with a mechanical valve. The 2020 ACC/AHA and 2021 ESC/EACTS guidelines remain cautious and position the Ross as an option in selected patients at experienced centers, while the 2025 EACTS expert consensus argues for broader use. Reasonable surgeons and cardiologists read the same data and reach different conclusions, and the gap between the guidelines and the consensus statement is itself a teaching point. [REVIEW]

**Reinforcement techniques.** External support grafts, the inclusion technique, annular stabilization, and reinforcement of the sinotubular junction are all used to prevent autograft dilation. There is no randomized comparison. Some surgeons argue that wrapping a living root in a synthetic graft defeats the purpose of a living valve and may alter leaflet mechanics, and a published commentary makes exactly that point. Others consider reinforcement mandatory in patients with aortic regurgitation and a dilated annulus. The German Ross Registry found that surgical technique was not an independent predictor of reoperation. [REVIEW]

**Blood pressure targets after the Ross.** Every Ross center controls blood pressure strictly, early and for life, on the physiological argument that a pulmonary root under systemic pressure dilates faster when the pressure is higher. The specific targets, the agents, and whether beta blockade is superior to other classes for the autograft are expert practice without trial evidence. Any number in this case must be the surgeon's and the institution's. [NMH protocol, insert]

**Whether the Ross should be done outside high-volume centers.** The 2026 North American analysis by Mazine and colleagues found operative mortality roughly threefold higher at centers performing one or two Ross procedures per year than at those performing more than ten, with a similar relationship for surgeon volume, and a rise in overall mortality after 2020 confined to low-volume centers. The counterargument is that volume thresholds restrict access and that outcomes at low-volume centers can be acceptable with proctoring. This is the live policy debate in the field. [REVIEW]

**Catheterization laboratory versus direct return to the operating room for day-1 coronary button ischemia.** There is no evidence base. Some surgeons go straight to the chest, others want the angiogram. Institutional practice should be written into this case. [NMH protocol, insert]
discussWithAttending: The surgeon wrote a systolic target for the first night. Defend it from first principles, then describe the patient in whom you would deliberately run above it.

On day 1 the angiogram shows a kink that improves with loading. The interventionalist has a stent ready and the surgeon is 40 minutes away. The patient is stable. Make the decision and justify it, then say what would have to change to reverse it.

A 29-year-old with aortic regurgitation and a bicuspid valve is in the highest-risk group for autograft dilation. Should that have argued against the Ross in the first place, or for reinforcement? Where would you draw the line?
The guidelines are cautious about the Ross and the EACTS consensus is enthusiastic. What would it take, in terms of evidence, for the guidelines to move, and is that evidence ever likely to exist?

This patient's anterior wall is stunned after a corrected button problem. Walk through which temporary mechanical support options would be acceptable in a patient with a fresh autograft root and a reimplanted left main, and which you would refuse.
